title: Toxicology II: Specific Poisonings
summary: Acetaminophen, salicylates, toxic alcohols, carbon monoxide, cyanide and heavy metals.

lessons.title: Acetaminophen and Salicylates

levels.kid:
**Acetaminophen** (also called paracetamol) and **aspirin** are medicines in almost every home. Used the right way, they help with pain and fever. But if a little kid finds the bottle and swallows a lot by accident, they can be dangerous.

Too much acetaminophen can hurt the **liver**, and the scary part is the person may feel fine at first. Doctors have a great antidote called **NAC** that protects the liver, and it works best if given early.

Too much aspirin makes people breathe fast, hear ringing in their ears, and feel very sick.

That's why medicines go up high and locked, and poison control gets called right away.
levels.hs:
**Acetaminophen (paracetamol)** is safe at the right amount but is a leading cause of acute liver failure in many countries, often through accidental or unintentional excess (for example, using two products that both contain it).

How it harms: most of the drug is safely conjugated in the liver. A small part is turned by CYP2E1 into a toxic product, **NAPQI**, which is normally neutralized by **glutathione**. When glutathione runs out, NAPQI damages liver cells.

The course has phases: early on people may have mild nausea or no symptoms at all; liver injury appears after a day or more. That silent start is why doctors check levels in any uncertain ingestion. A blood level taken at the right time is plotted on a **nomogram** to decide whether to treat with **N-acetylcysteine (NAC)**, which refills glutathione. NAC is nearly fully protective when started early.

**Salicylates (aspirin, oil of wintergreen)** cause:
- **Tinnitus** (ringing ears), nausea and vomiting.
- **Fast, deep breathing**, because salicylate stimulates the brain's breathing center (respiratory alkalosis).
- A **metabolic acidosis**, because it disrupts energy production in mitochondria.
- Fever, confusion and, in severe cases, brain swelling and fluid in the lungs.

Concentrated oil of wintergreen is especially dangerous to children. Treatment includes fluids, **sodium bicarbonate** to alkalinize the blood and urine, correcting potassium, and **hemodialysis** in severe cases.
levels.college:
**Acetaminophen.** At therapeutic exposure, glucuronidation and sulfation dominate; a minority undergoes CYP2E1 (and 3A4/1A2) oxidation to NAPQI, conjugated by glutathione to mercapturic acid. In toxicity, conjugation pathways saturate, more drug is shunted to NAPQI, glutathione falls, and NAPQI arylates mitochondrial proteins, causing oxidative stress and **centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis**, where CYP2E1 is concentrated and oxygen tension is lowest. Stages: (1) asymptomatic or mild GI upset; (2) rising transaminases from about a day after ingestion; (3) peak hepatotoxicity days later with coagulopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, renal injury; (4) recovery or death/transplant.

Risk assessment for a single acute ingestion uses a level drawn at or after the 4-hour mark plotted on the **Rumack–Matthew nomogram**; above the treatment line, give NAC. The nomogram does not apply to staggered or repeated ingestions or unknown timing, which are managed by levels plus transaminases. **NAC** (IV or oral) is most effective early but helps even after liver injury begins. Poor-prognosis markers inform transplant referral (King's College criteria: acidosis, coagulopathy, creatinine, encephalopathy).

**Salicylates.** Salicylate directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center (early respiratory alkalosis) and **uncouples oxidative phosphorylation**, increasing oxygen consumption, heat production and lactate, plus accumulation of organic acids: a **mixed respiratory alkalosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis** in adults (children may present with acidosis predominantly). Other features: tinnitus, hyperthermia, hypoglycemia in the brain despite normal serum glucose (neuroglycopenia), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, cerebral edema. Acidemia shifts salicylate into its non-ionized, lipophilic form, which enters the CNS, so worsening acidosis is lethal.

Management: fluids, glucose in altered patients, **sodium bicarbonate** (serum and urine alkalinization), potassium repletion, serial levels (absorption may be prolonged), and **hemodialysis** for altered mental status, severe acidosis, kidney failure, pulmonary edema or rising levels despite treatment.
levels.phd:
**Zonal biology of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.** Hepatic lobules are metabolically zoned along the portal-to-central axis: CYP2E1 and glutamine synthetase are pericentral (zone 3), while glutathione stores are relatively lower there. NAPQI forms protein adducts predominantly with mitochondrial proteins; the ensuing superoxide and peroxynitrite formation triggers a self-amplifying loop involving JNK phosphorylation and translocation to mitochondria (via Sab), mitochondrial permeability transition, and release of endonuclease G and AIF, causing nuclear DNA fragmentation and **regulated necrosis** rather than classical apoptosis. Damage-associated molecular patterns then recruit innate immunity, which both amplifies injury and orchestrates repair. Acetaminophen–protein adducts measured in serum serve as specific biomarkers of exposure, helpful when histories are unclear.

**Modifiers of susceptibility.** Glutathione depletion (malnutrition, prolonged fasting) and CYP2E1 induction (certain drugs such as isoniazid) are discussed as risk modifiers; the clinical weight of each is debated, and current guidance generally uses the standard nomogram line regardless. Research on new adjuncts (fomepizole as CYP2E1 and JNK inhibitor, calmangafodipir as a superoxide dismutase mimetic) targets massive exposures where NAC alone may be insufficient.

**Salicylate pharmacology at toxic exposure.** Salicylate shows saturable glycine conjugation (to salicyluric acid) and glucuronidation, converting elimination from first-order to zero-order kinetics, so half-life lengthens dramatically. Protein binding saturates, raising the free fraction. Uncoupling arises because salicylate is a lipophilic weak acid that shuttles protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, dissipating the gradient used by ATP synthase. Pill bezoars and enteric-coated formulations produce delayed peaks.

**Acid–base logic.** Henderson–Hasselbalch predicts that each fall in blood pH increases non-ionized salicylate, which crosses the blood–brain barrier; CSF salicylate correlates with mortality better than serum levels. Hence the clinical priority of preventing acidemia, including during intubation.
levels.expert:
**Acetaminophen practice points:**
- Get the time of ingestion as precisely as possible; plot a level drawn at or after 4 hours on the nomogram for single acute ingestions.
- If timing is unknown or the ingestion was repeated over time (for example, a child given too much by mistake over several days, or an adult using two products containing the same drug), treat based on detectable acetaminophen or abnormal transaminases, with toxicology input.
- Do not wait for a level to start NAC if presentation is late or the level will be delayed beyond the early window.
- IV NAC can cause anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, wheeze), usually managed by pausing and restarting more slowly; it is not a true allergy.
- Endpoints for stopping NAC: acetaminophen undetectable and transaminases normal or improving, with improving INR.
- Refer early to a liver transplant center when poor prognostic features appear.

**Pediatric safety:** liquid formulations come in different concentrations; dosing-device mix-ups are a known source of error, so syringes matched to the product are used, and caregivers check every combination product's ingredient list.

**Salicylate practice points:**
- Think of salicylates in any unexplained mixed acid–base disorder, tachypnea with acidosis, or unexplained fever and confusion in an older adult on chronic aspirin (chronic toxicity is often missed and has higher mortality at lower measured levels).
- Measure levels serially until clearly falling; check that units are correct (laboratories report differently).
- Bicarbonate infusion targets alkaline urine while avoiding excessive serum alkalemia; replace potassium.
- Give glucose to altered patients even with normal blood glucose (brain neuroglycopenia).
- Call nephrology early. If intubation is unavoidable, hyperventilate to match pre-intubation compensation and consider dialysis around the procedure.
- Topical salicylates (oil of wintergreen, some liniments) are underestimated household dangers for children.

Always involve poison control; both poisonings are common, treatable and unforgiving when recognized late.

keyPoints: Acetaminophen → NAPQI (CYP2E1); glutathione depletion → zone 3 necrosis
Early course silent; check levels; Rumack–Matthew nomogram for single acute ingestions
NAC is nearly fully protective early and still helps late
Salicylates: tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis + AG metabolic acidosis, uncoupling, hyperthermia
Treat salicylates with bicarbonate, potassium, glucose and dialysis when severe; avoid acidemia

lessons.title: Toxic Alcohols

levels.kid:
Some liquids in the garage or kitchen have names with "alcohol" or "glycol" in them, like **antifreeze** for cars or **windshield washer fluid**. They are not drinks at all. Some even taste sweet, which is why they must be kept away from kids and pets.

If someone swallows them by accident, the body turns them into **acids** that can hurt the eyes, the kidneys and the brain.

Doctors have a medicine called **fomepizole** that stops the body from making those acids. They can also use a **dialysis machine** to clean the blood.

So: call poison control fast, even if the person feels okay.
levels.hs:
**Toxic alcohols** are chemicals found in household and industrial products, accidentally swallowed by children or mistaken for something else.
- **Methanol**: windshield washer fluid, some fuels, solvents.
- **Ethylene glycol**: antifreeze (it can taste sweet).
- **Isopropanol**: rubbing alcohol, some hand sanitizers.

The parent chemicals are not very toxic themselves. The danger comes from what the liver turns them into, starting with the enzyme **alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)**:
- Methanol → **formic acid**, which damages the **optic nerve** (vision loss, "snowfield" vision) and deep brain areas.
- Ethylene glycol → **glycolic acid** and **oxalic acid**. Oxalate binds calcium, forming crystals that damage the **kidneys** and lowering blood calcium.
- Isopropanol → **acetone**, causing sleepiness and a fruity breath smell but usually **no acidosis**.

Lab clues:
- Early: a high **osmolar gap** (extra dissolved particles from the alcohol).
- Later: a high **anion gap metabolic acidosis** (from the acids).
- Ethylene glycol: calcium oxalate crystals in urine.

Treatment:
- **Fomepizole** blocks ADH, so no toxic acids form.
- **Hemodialysis** removes the alcohol and its acids and fixes acidosis.
- Vitamins help detox pathways: **folate** for methanol; **thiamine** and **pyridoxine** for ethylene glycol.

Because early patients may look well, a suspected exposure always means calling poison control and getting tested.
levels.college:
**Metabolism.** Methanol and ethylene glycol are oxidized by **alcohol dehydrogenase** to aldehydes and then by **aldehyde dehydrogenase** to acids.
- Methanol → formaldehyde → **formic acid**. Formate inhibits **cytochrome c oxidase**, causing histotoxic hypoxia, particularly in the optic nerve (papilledema, hyperemic discs, blindness) and **basal ganglia (putaminal necrosis, sometimes hemorrhage)**. Formate is cleared by folate-dependent conversion to CO₂ and water, so folinic or folic acid is given.
- Ethylene glycol → glycoaldehyde → **glycolic acid** (main acidosis driver) → glyoxylic acid → **oxalic acid**. Oxalate precipitates as **calcium oxalate monohydrate** crystals in renal tubules (acute kidney injury) and elsewhere, causing hypocalcemia (QT prolongation, tetany). Thiamine and pyridoxine shunt glyoxylate toward non-toxic products (α-hydroxy-β-ketoadipate and glycine).
- **Isopropanol** → **acetone** (a ketone, not an acid): CNS depression, hemorrhagic gastritis, ketosis without acidosis, elevated osmolar gap; treatment is supportive.
- **Diethylene glycol** (contaminant in improperly manufactured medicines, behind historical mass poisonings) → diglycolic acid: acute kidney injury and a delayed cranial and peripheral neuropathy.
- **Propylene glycol** (vehicle in some IV medications): lactic acidosis with prolonged high-volume infusions.

**Diagnosis.** Direct measurement (gas chromatography) is definitive but often unavailable quickly. The **osmolar gap** (measured − calculated osmolality) rises early; the **anion gap** rises as acids accumulate. A normal osmolar gap does not exclude exposure. Lactate may be falsely elevated by glycolate on some analyzers (the "lactate gap"). Urine fluorescence under ultraviolet light (from antifreeze dye) is unreliable.

**Treatment.**
- **Fomepizole** (competitive ADH inhibitor) as soon as exposure is suspected; ethanol is a historical alternative competing substrate, now rarely used because of monitoring burden.
- **Hemodialysis** for severe acidosis, visual changes, kidney failure, deteriorating status or high measured levels; it removes parent and metabolites.
- **Bicarbonate** for severe acidemia (reduces formate entry into tissues).
- **Cofactors:** folate (methanol); thiamine and pyridoxine (ethylene glycol).
levels.phd:
**Why the parent is benign and the metabolite lethal.** This is metabolic activation in its purest form: the clinical toxicity is time-lagged by ADH kinetics, and blocking the first enzymatic step converts a lethal poison into a slowly excreted, relatively inert solvent. Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) binds ADH with far higher affinity than ethanol, without causing CNS depression. With ADH blocked, methanol's elimination becomes very slow (renal and pulmonary), and ethylene glycol is renally cleared if kidney function is preserved; this distinction shapes whether dialysis is needed for kinetics alone.

**Formate neurotoxicity.** Formate inhibits complex IV, reduces ATP and causes axoplasmic flow stasis in the retrolaminar optic nerve, producing optic disc edema. The putamen's high metabolic demand and venous drainage pattern render it vulnerable; MRI shows bilateral putaminal necrosis, sometimes hemorrhagic, and subcortical white-matter lesions, and survivors may develop parkinsonism. Primates are uniquely susceptible because of low hepatic tetrahydrofolate levels, explaining why rodent models poorly predicted human methanol toxicity.

**Oxalate deposition.** Calcium oxalate monohydrate (needle-shaped) is more characteristic of ethylene glycol than dihydrate (envelope-shaped), but crystals are neither sensitive nor specific. Glycolate oxidase inhibition and oxalate crystal adhesion to tubular epithelium are areas of mechanistic research. Cranial neuropathies (facial, vestibulocochlear) can appear days later.

**Gap kinetics.** As metabolism proceeds, each mole of alcohol converted to acid shifts from osmolar to anion gap. The osmolar gap is insensitive (the population normal range is wide, and an individual's baseline is unknown), and other substances (ethanol, mannitol, ketones in some states, lactate) raise it.

**Mass poisonings.** Diethylene glycol substituted for glycerin or propylene glycol in medicines has repeatedly caused mass pediatric deaths, from the 1937 sulfanilamide elixir tragedy (which led to modern US drug safety law) to recent cough syrup contaminations. Regulatory toxicology is born from such events.
levels.expert:
**Clinical approach to suspected toxic alcohol exposure.** Typical scenarios: a toddler who drank from an unlabeled container, windshield washer fluid stored in a drink bottle, an occupational splash or inhalation, or a contaminated product. Call poison control and start fomepizole on suspicion when exposure is plausible, rather than waiting for confirmatory levels, which many hospitals send out and receive days later.

**What experienced clinicians watch:**
- **Anion gap acidosis without a clear cause** (no lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis or uremia to explain it) triggers a toxic alcohol workup.
- **Visual symptoms** (blurring, central scotoma, "snowstorm" vision) or fundoscopic disc edema suggest methanol and push toward urgent dialysis.
- **Hypocalcemia and kidney injury** suggest ethylene glycol.
- **Ketones without acidosis** and an osmolar gap suggest isopropanol.
- Repeat osmolality, gases and electrolytes over hours, because the picture evolves.

**Dialysis decisions** weigh acidosis severity, end-organ effects, measured levels when available and kidney function. Fomepizole is continued (with adjustment during dialysis because it is dialyzable) until the alcohol is cleared and acidosis has resolved.

**Neuroimaging:** methanol survivors with persistent deficits show bilateral putaminal lesions; hemorrhagic transformation can complicate anticoagulation used during dialysis.

**Pitfalls:**
- A falsely high lactate from glycolate interference can lead to misdiagnosis as sepsis or shock.
- Treating with bicarbonate alone without fomepizole lets toxic acids keep forming.
- Missing co-exposures in workplace incidents (solvent mixtures).

**Prevention:** store chemicals in original, labeled containers, never in drink bottles; some antifreeze products add bittering agents to deter accidental ingestion by children and pets.

keyPoints: Methanol → formic acid: optic nerve and putamen injury; give folate
Ethylene glycol → glycolic and oxalic acids: acidosis, oxalate crystals, kidney injury, hypocalcemia
Isopropanol → acetone: ketosis without acidosis
Osmolar gap early, anion gap later; a normal osmolar gap doesn't exclude exposure
Fomepizole blocks ADH; dialysis removes alcohol and acids

lessons.title: Carbon Monoxide and Cyanide

levels.kid:
**Carbon monoxide** is a sneaky gas. You can't see it or smell it. It comes from things that burn fuel, like a broken heater, a car running in a closed garage, or a generator indoors.

Your red blood cells carry oxygen like little delivery trucks. Carbon monoxide jumps into the trucks and won't get out, so there's no room for oxygen. People get headaches, feel sick and sleepy, and can pass out.

The fix: get into fresh air, call for help, and doctors give lots of oxygen.

**Cyanide**, which can come from smoke in fires, stops cells from using oxygen at all. It has a special antidote that grabs it.

A **CO alarm** at home keeps everyone safe.
levels.hs:
**Carbon monoxide (CO)** is a colorless, odorless gas from incomplete combustion: faulty furnaces, indoor generators, blocked chimneys, cars in garages, house fires. It is a leading cause of accidental poisoning, especially in winter and after power outages.

How it harms:
- It binds **hemoglobin** about 200–250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming **carboxyhemoglobin**, so less oxygen is carried.
- It makes the remaining hemoglobin hold oxygen more tightly (a **left shift**), so tissues get even less.
- It also poisons mitochondria and triggers brain inflammation.

Symptoms are vague: headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion, like the flu. A clue is that several people in the same house, or the pets, get sick together. Normal **pulse oximeters cannot tell** carboxyhemoglobin from oxygenated hemoglobin, so they read falsely normal. A blood test called **co-oximetry** measures it.

Treatment: remove from the source, high-flow **oxygen** (which speeds CO removal), and sometimes **hyperbaric oxygen**. Some survivors develop memory or movement problems weeks later.

**Cyanide** blocks **cytochrome c oxidase** in mitochondria, so cells cannot use oxygen even when plenty is delivered. Sources: smoke from burning plastics and fabrics in house fires, industrial chemicals, and certain plant seeds and kernels. Signs: sudden collapse, seizures, very high lactate. The first-line antidote is **hydroxocobalamin**, which binds cyanide to form vitamin B12.
levels.college:
**Carbon monoxide pathophysiology.** CO binds the heme iron of hemoglobin with roughly 200–250-fold greater affinity than O₂ and stabilizes the relaxed (R) state, shifting the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve **left** and making it more hyperbolic, which impairs unloading. CO also binds myoglobin (myocardial dysfunction), cytochrome c oxidase (impaired oxidative phosphorylation) and activates platelets and neutrophils, causing lipid peroxidation and immune-mediated brain injury. This explains why carboxyhemoglobin levels correlate poorly with outcomes.

**Clinical features:** headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion, syncope, seizures, coma, myocardial ischemia and arrhythmias, lactic acidosis. "Cherry-red" skin is rare and late. **Delayed neurological sequelae** (cognitive deficits, parkinsonism, mood change) may appear days to weeks later; MRI classically shows **bilateral globus pallidus** lesions and white-matter changes.

**Diagnosis:** **co-oximetry** (arterial or venous) measures carboxyhemoglobin; standard pulse oximetry overestimates saturation. Interpret levels with timing and oxygen exposure in mind. Check ECG and troponin; screen household members.

**Treatment:** high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask shortens carboxyhemoglobin half-life substantially compared with room air; **hyperbaric oxygen** shortens it further and may reduce delayed sequelae in selected patients (loss of consciousness, neurological deficits, cardiac ischemia, pregnancy), though trial evidence is mixed. Fetal hemoglobin binds CO avidly and clears slowly, so pregnancy lowers the threshold for hyperbaric therapy.

**Cyanide.** CN⁻ binds the ferric iron (heme a₃) of **cytochrome c oxidase** (complex IV), halting oxidative phosphorylation: histotoxic hypoxia with **severe lactic acidosis**, raised venous oxygen saturation ("arterialized" venous blood), seizures, coma and cardiovascular collapse. Sources: **smoke inhalation** (often combined with CO), industrial exposures, prolonged nitroprusside infusions, and cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin in apricot kernels, poorly processed cassava).

**Antidotes:**
- **Hydroxocobalamin:** binds cyanide to form renally excreted cyanocobalamin; first-line, safe in smoke inhalation. Causes red skin and urine, and interferes with colorimetric labs and hemodialysis machine blood-leak alarms.
- **Nitrites** (amyl, sodium) induce methemoglobinemia, which pulls cyanide off cytochrome oxidase; dangerous with concurrent CO (further reduces oxygen carrying).
- **Sodium thiosulfate:** sulfur donor for **rhodanese**, converting cyanide to thiocyanate.
levels.phd:
**Molecular selectivity of CO and its consequences.** Free heme binds CO about 20,000 times better than O₂; the distal histidine in hemoglobin's pocket sterically and electrostatically disfavors CO's linear binding geometry, lowering the preference to the roughly 200–250-fold seen clinically. This protein-imposed discrimination is a classic structural biology case study. Endogenous CO from heme oxygenase is a gasotransmitter with anti-inflammatory and vasodilatory signaling roles, so physiology and toxicology lie on one continuum.

**Mechanisms of delayed neurological sequelae.** Beyond hypoxia, CO causes perivascular platelet–neutrophil interactions, myeloperoxidase release, and oxidative modification of myelin basic protein, which then triggers an adaptive autoimmune response against myelin (shown in rodent models). The globus pallidus is vulnerable because of its high iron content and border-zone perfusion. Hyperbaric oxygen may inhibit neutrophil β2-integrin adhesion, a proposed mechanism for reduced sequelae; the Weaver trial supported benefit, whereas other trials did not, and debates center on protocol and timing differences.

**Cyanide biochemistry.** Cyanide's affinity for the oxidized a₃ copper/iron binuclear center halts electron flow, collapsing the proton gradient; cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis (lactate surge). Lactate in smoke-inhalation victims correlates with cyanide exposure and is used as a surrogate when cyanide levels (slow to measure) are unavailable. Endogenous detoxification by rhodanese (mitochondrial sulfurtransferase) is limited by sulfur donor availability, hence thiosulfate's role, though its onset is slow. Hydroxocobalamin's cobalt binds cyanide with very high affinity, forming a stable complex without inducing methemoglobin, which is why it suits fire victims who also have carboxyhemoglobinemia.

**Hydrogen sulfide** shares the complex IV mechanism (sewer and manure-pit exposures, with rapid "knockdown"); it is relatively quickly detoxified, so supportive care dominates.

**Nitroprusside** releases cyanide as it is metabolized; prolonged or high-rate infusion, especially with low thiosulfate reserves, risks toxicity, which is why it is sometimes co-administered with thiosulfate and monitored.
levels.expert:
**Recognizing CO poisoning** requires suspicion. Clues: flu-like illness in several household members at once, symptoms that improve away from home, pets ill, winter heating season, recent power outage with a generator, and fire exposure. Ask about heating sources. Emergency medical services and fire crews may carry CO detectors on their bags.

**Workup:** co-oximetry, ECG, troponin, lactate, pregnancy test where relevant, and a careful neurological and cognitive exam documented at baseline. Remember standard pulse oximetry is misleading. Note how long the patient has been on oxygen before the level was drawn, because levels fall quickly with treatment.

**Hyperbaric oxygen decisions** are made with a hyperbaric center: considered for loss of consciousness, neurological deficits, cardiac ischemia, severe acidosis, pregnancy or persistent symptoms. Transfer logistics should not delay high-flow oxygen.

**Follow-up:** arrange cognitive follow-up for delayed sequelae, and confirm the home source was fixed and a working CO alarm installed before discharge; families are often discharged back into the exposure.

**Smoke inhalation:** suspect cyanide in a fire victim with altered consciousness, hypotension, seizures, or a markedly elevated lactate. Give **hydroxocobalamin** empirically without waiting for cyanide levels. Avoid nitrites, because methemoglobin plus carboxyhemoglobin is deadly. Secure the airway early when thermal injury signs appear (stridor, soot, facial burns).

**Practical antidote issues:** draw blood for labs before hydroxocobalamin when possible, because it colors serum and disrupts colorimetric assays; warn dialysis teams about false blood-leak alarms.

**Industrial and agricultural settings:** responders must protect themselves first; in confined spaces (manure pits, sewers), multiple rescuers have died attempting rescue without breathing apparatus.

**Prevention messaging** is part of the job: alarms on every floor, annual furnace checks, generators outdoors away from windows, and never warming up cars in closed garages.

keyPoints: CO: odorless; binds Hb ~200–250× O₂; left shift; mitochondrial and immune injury
Pulse oximetry misleads; use co-oximetry; suspect when a household is sick together
Treat CO with high-flow oxygen; hyperbaric oxygen in selected patients; watch delayed sequelae (globus pallidus)
Cyanide blocks complex IV → lactic acidosis, arterialized venous blood

lessons.title: Heavy Metals

levels.kid:
**Heavy metals** like **lead**, **mercury** and **arsenic** are found in nature, but they don't belong inside our bodies.

Lead can come from **old paint** chips and dust in very old houses. Mercury is in some old thermometers and in certain big fish. Arsenic can sneak into some well water.

These metals are bad guests: they move in, stay a long time, and mess up the body's machines, especially the **brain** and **nerves**. Kids' growing brains are most at risk.

Doctors find the metal with blood or urine tests, remove the source, and sometimes give a **chelator**, a medicine that grabs the metal and carries it out.
levels.hs:
**Heavy metal poisoning** is usually environmental or occupational, and slow rather than sudden.

- **Lead:** old paint dust (especially during renovation), contaminated soil, some imported pottery, spices or remedies, and old water pipes. Children absorb more and are most vulnerable. Effects: learning and attention problems, belly pain, constipation, **anemia** with **basophilic stippling** of red cells, and in severe cases brain swelling. Adults may get nerve problems such as **wrist drop**. Treatment: remove the source; chelation (succimer, or BAL plus CaNa₂EDTA when severe).
- **Mercury** comes in three forms. Elemental vapor (broken thermometers, some industrial uses) is dangerous when **inhaled**, harming lungs and brain. Inorganic salts harm the gut and **kidneys**. Organic **methylmercury** builds up in large predatory fish and damages the developing **nervous system** (the Minamata disaster).
- **Arsenic:** contaminated groundwater in some regions, industrial exposure. Acute: vomiting, diarrhea, heart rhythm problems. Chronic: skin darkening, thickened palms and soles, **Mees lines** on nails, painful **peripheral neuropathy** and cancers.
- **Thallium:** rare, causes dramatic **hair loss** and painful neuropathy; treated with **Prussian blue**.

Testing depends on the metal: blood for lead and methylmercury, urine for inorganic mercury and arsenic.

Fun fact with a twist: **arsenic trioxide** is a real cancer drug for a type of leukemia (acute promyelocytic leukemia). The difference between medicine and poison is context and careful use.
levels.college:
**Lead.** Pb²⁺ substitutes for Ca²⁺ and Zn²⁺. It inhibits **δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase** and **ferrochelatase**, raising ALA and **zinc protoporphyrin**, producing microcytic anemia; it inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, causing **basophilic stippling**. Neurotoxicity: NMDA receptor antagonism during development, impaired synaptic pruning and plasticity, and blood–brain barrier damage. Children: cognitive deficits and behavioral problems; severe exposure causes **lead encephalopathy** with raised intracranial pressure. Adults: peripheral motor neuropathy (wrist and foot drop), hypertension, nephropathy, gout ("saturnine gout"). X-rays may show dense metaphyseal **lead lines** in children. Most body lead is in bone, with slow release. Diagnosis: venous blood lead. Treatment: source removal (essential), iron and calcium sufficiency, chelation (succimer orally; BAL then CaNa₂EDTA for encephalopathy).

**Mercury.**
- Elemental (Hg⁰): poorly absorbed orally, well absorbed by inhalation (vapor), lipophilic, crosses the blood–brain barrier, oxidized to Hg²⁺ in tissues: acute pneumonitis; chronic tremor, gingivitis and **erethism** (irritability, shyness).
- Inorganic (Hg²⁺ salts): corrosive gastroenteritis and **acute tubular necrosis**.
- Organic (methylmercury): efficiently absorbed, crosses the placenta and blood–brain barrier via the L-type amino acid transporter (as a cysteine conjugate mimicking methionine): visual field constriction, ataxia, paresthesias, and severe fetal neurodevelopmental injury.
- Chelators: DMSA/DMPS for elemental and inorganic forms; chelation is of limited benefit for methylmercury.

**Arsenic.** Trivalent arsenite binds sulfhydryl groups, notably **lipoic acid** in pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, impairing the Krebs cycle; pentavalent arsenate substitutes for phosphate (arsenolysis). Acute: rice-water diarrhea, hypotension, **QT prolongation and torsades**, later encephalopathy and an ascending sensorimotor neuropathy that can mimic Guillain–Barré syndrome. Chronic: hyperpigmentation, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, Mees lines, skin, lung and bladder cancers. Diagnosis: speciated urine arsenic (seafood arsenobetaine is non-toxic). Chelation: BAL, DMSA or DMPS.

**Thallium:** alopecia, painful ascending neuropathy; Prussian blue. **Cadmium:** renal tubular dysfunction and bone disease (itai-itai disease).
levels.phd:
**Metal toxicity as coordination chemistry.** Toxicity follows from ionic mimicry and ligand preference. Lead mimics divalent cations at calcium-binding proteins (calmodulin, synaptotagmin, protein kinase C), perturbing neurotransmitter release at picomolar free concentrations, and displaces zinc from zinc-finger proteins, including ALAD. Methylmercury–cysteine is a structural mimic of methionine, hijacking LAT1 transport across the blood–brain barrier and placenta (molecular mimicry). Thallium (Tl⁺) mimics K⁺, entering cells via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and disrupting potassium-dependent processes, including ribosomal function, and binds riboflavin, explaining neuropathy and hair loss. Arsenate mimics phosphate, uncoupling ATP synthesis by forming unstable ADP-arsenate that hydrolyzes spontaneously.

**Developmental neurotoxicology.** Lead and methylmercury exert their greatest harm during periods of synaptogenesis and myelination. Population studies of blood lead show a supralinear dose–response relationship: the steepest per-unit decline in IQ occurs at the lowest exposures, a finding that drove reference values ever lower and ended the concept of a safe level. Minamata (industrial methylmercury discharge in the 1950s) revealed fetal vulnerability: mothers with mild symptoms bore children with severe cerebral palsy-like syndromes, because the fetal brain concentrated methylmercury.

**Thimerosal** contains ethylmercury, which has a much shorter half-life and different kinetics from methylmercury; large epidemiological studies found no link to neurodevelopmental disorders, and its precautionary removal from most childhood vaccines was not based on evidence of harm.

**Arsenic as a drug.** Arsenic trioxide induces degradation of the PML–RARα fusion oncoprotein (binding PML zinc fingers, promoting SUMOylation and ubiquitin-mediated degradation); combined with all-trans retinoic acid, it cures most acute promyelocytic leukemia, a remarkable reversal from poison to precision therapy. Its QT liability is the same physiology seen in poisoning.

**Biomarkers.** Hair and nail testing are vulnerable to external contamination; commercial "provoked urine" chelation challenge tests are invalid and can harm. Validated specimens: blood lead, blood methylmercury, urine inorganic mercury, speciated urine arsenic.
levels.expert:
**How clinicians approach suspected metal exposure.** Start with the exposure history: housing age and renovations, hobbies (stained glass, firearms ranges, ceramics glazing, fishing weights), occupation (battery recycling, smelting, mining, dentistry with mercury), imported foods, cosmetics, spices and traditional remedies, and water source (private wells). Children's pica and hand-to-mouth behavior matter. Map the timing to symptoms.

**Pattern recognition:**
- Microcytic anemia, abdominal pain, constipation and developmental concerns in a toddler from an older home: lead.
- Tremor, irritability and gingivitis in a worker exposed to vapor: elemental mercury.
- Painful ascending neuropathy weeks after severe gastroenteritis, with Mees lines: arsenic (an important Guillain–Barré mimic).
- Severe hair loss with painful neuropathy: thallium.

**Lab strategy:** test the right specimen for the suspected species; avoid unvalidated hair analysis and provoked urine tests. For arsenic, request speciation, because recent seafood raises total urine arsenic with non-toxic organic forms.

**Management principles:**
- Source identification and removal comes first, with public-health and occupational-health involvement; screen siblings and coworkers.
- Chelate selectively, for clear clinical toxicity or significantly elevated levels, under toxicology guidance.
- Correct iron deficiency and ensure adequate calcium in lead-exposed children.
- Arsenic: cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation, electrolyte correction, avoid other QT-prolonging drugs.
- Lead encephalopathy: intensive care, seizure control, management of raised intracranial pressure, and chelation; neurosurgical decompression is not the solution, because the brain swelling is metabolic.

**Broken mercury thermometer at home:** ventilate, do not vacuum (which aerosolizes vapor), and follow local guidance for cleanup; small household spills are rarely dangerous when handled properly.

**Long-term follow-up:** developmental surveillance for exposed children; neuropathy rehabilitation; cancer surveillance after chronic arsenic exposure.

keyPoints: Lead: paint dust; inhibits ALAD and ferrochelatase; stippling; neurocognitive harm; no safe level
Mercury: vapor (lungs/brain), inorganic (kidney), methylmercury (fetal brain, fish)
Arsenic: binds lipoic acid; QT prolongation; Mees lines; neuropathy; speciate urine
Thallium: alopecia + neuropathy; Prussian blue
Remove the source first; chelate selectively; avoid hair and provoked-urine tests

lessons.title: Cardiotoxic Drug Overdoses

levels.kid:
Some heart medicines are very helpful when taken the right way, but can be dangerous if someone takes too much **by accident**, like a little kid who finds grandma's pills, or a mix-up at home.

The heart has an electric beat, like a drummer keeping time. Too much of some medicines can make the drummer go **too slow**, **too fast**, or **out of rhythm**.

Doctors watch the heartbeat on a screen called an **ECG**. They have special antidotes: one catches too much **digoxin**, and others help the heart squeeze harder.

This is why all medicines, even heart ones, must be kept locked and out of reach.
levels.hs:
Cardiotoxic drug poisoning usually happens through **accidental ingestion by children**, **medication errors**, **drug interactions** or **kidney decline** that lets a drug build up. Some adult heart pills are especially dangerous to toddlers.

- **Beta-blockers** (e.g., propranolol, metoprolol): slow heart rate, low blood pressure, low blood sugar in children; propranolol can cause seizures. Treatment: fluids, **glucagon**, **high-insulin euglycemia therapy**, vasopressors.
- **Calcium channel blockers** (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem, amlodipine): low blood pressure, slow heart (verapamil/diltiazem), and **high blood sugar**. Treatment: **calcium**, high-insulin therapy, vasopressors.
- **Digoxin**: nausea, vomiting, **yellow-green vision**, confusion, many types of arrhythmias, and **high potassium** in acute poisoning. Antidote: **digoxin immune Fab**. Chronic toxicity often follows kidney decline or interacting drugs.
- **Tricyclic antidepressants** (e.g., amitriptyline): block heart **sodium channels**, causing a **wide QRS**, plus seizures, low blood pressure and anticholinergic signs. Treatment: **sodium bicarbonate**.
- **QT-prolonging drugs** (many antibiotics, antipsychotics, antiemetics): risk **torsades de pointes**; treatment includes **magnesium**.
- **Local anesthetics** (e.g., bupivacaine) accidentally entering a vein: seizures and cardiac arrest; treated with **lipid emulsion**.

The ECG is the key test: heart rate, PR, QRS and QT intervals all give clues. As always, call poison control and get emergency help right away.
levels.college:
**Beta-blockers.** Reduced cAMP lowers chronotropy, inotropy and AV conduction; hypoglycemia (especially children) from impaired glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Propranolol is lipophilic and blocks sodium channels (QRS widening, seizures); sotalol blocks potassium channels (QT prolongation, torsades). Therapy: atropine (often ineffective), fluids, calcium, **glucagon** (Gs-coupled glucagon receptor bypass; vomiting common), **high-insulin euglycemia therapy (HIET)**, catecholamines, pacing, and **VA-ECMO** for refractory shock.

**Calcium channel blockers.** L-type channel blockade reduces myocardial contractility and pacemaker activity (non-dihydropyridines: verapamil, diltiazem) and causes vasodilation (dihydropyridines: amlodipine, nifedipine, with reflex tachycardia until selectivity is lost at high exposure). Pancreatic β-cell L-type blockade reduces insulin release, causing **hyperglycemia** that correlates with severity. Myocardial insulin resistance and carbohydrate dependence underlie HIET's effectiveness. Sustained-release preparations produce delayed, prolonged toxicity; whole bowel irrigation may be considered.

**Digoxin.** Inhibits **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase**, raising intracellular Na⁺ and, via the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger, Ca²⁺ (positive inotropy), with increased vagal tone. Toxicity: increased automaticity plus AV nodal block, producing **bidirectional ventricular tachycardia**, atrial tachycardia with block, junctional rhythms, ventricular ectopy. Acute toxicity: **hyperkalemia** (prognostic, from pump inhibition). Chronic toxicity: often normal or low potassium, precipitated by renal decline, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or interacting drugs (amiodarone, verapamil, clarithromycin, which raise levels via P-gp inhibition). **Digoxin immune Fab** for life-threatening arrhythmias, significant hyperkalemia, or end-organ dysfunction.

**Sodium channel blockers** (tricyclics, flecainide, propranolol, diphenhydramine): **QRS widening**, **terminal R wave in aVR**, rightward terminal axis, ventricular tachycardia, hypotension. **Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate** provides sodium load and alkalemia, reducing drug binding to the channel. Tricyclics add α1 blockade, anticholinergic toxidrome and seizures.

**QT prolongation (hERG/IKr blockade):** torsades de pointes; treat with **magnesium sulfate**, correct potassium, overdrive pacing or isoproterenol for bradycardia-dependent torsades.

**Local anesthetic systemic toxicity:** CNS excitation then cardiovascular collapse (bupivacaine particularly cardiotoxic); **intravenous lipid emulsion** plus modified resuscitation.
levels.phd:
**Electrophysiologic logic.** Phase 0 depolarization depends on fast Na⁺ channels; blockade slows conduction (QRS widening) with use dependence: drugs with slow unbinding kinetics (class IC, tricyclics) accumulate block at faster heart rates, which is why tachycardia worsens QRS widening and why sinus tachycardia with a wide QRS can be misread as VT. Bicarbonate's benefit results from both the sodium gradient and alkalemia-induced reduction in the ionized, channel-binding fraction (changing drug–channel affinity), a rationale supported by experimental models showing that hypertonic saline also narrows QRS, but less so.

**Repolarization reserve.** IKr (hERG) blockade prolongs action potential duration heterogeneously across the myocardial wall, enabling early afterdepolarizations (via L-type Ca²⁺ reactivation) and transmural dispersion of repolarization, the substrate for torsades. Risk is amplified by bradycardia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, female sex, congenital long QT variants and drug interactions raising exposure (CYP3A4 inhibition). hERG's large inner cavity with aromatic residues (Y652, F656) explains its promiscuous binding of structurally diverse drugs, a central problem in drug development and why hERG screening is mandatory preclinically.

**Digoxin's narrow window.** Digoxin binds the α subunit of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in competition with extracellular K⁺: hypokalemia increases binding and toxicity, whereas acute toxicity raises serum K⁺. Fab fragments bind digoxin with higher affinity than the pump, creating a gradient that pulls digoxin from tissue receptors.

**Metabolic resuscitation.** In calcium channel blocker and β-blocker shock, the stressed myocardium shifts from fatty acid to carbohydrate oxidation yet becomes insulin resistant; high-insulin therapy improves myocardial glucose uptake, contractility and microvascular perfusion, with effects that lag, so early initiation is favored. Its effects are inotropic rather than chronotropic.

**Lipid emulsion mechanisms** include the lipid sink (partitioning lipophilic drug), fatty acid supply to the energy-starved myocardium, and direct effects on calcium handling; robust benefit is established for local anesthetic toxicity, with uncertain value elsewhere and potential interference with laboratory testing and ECMO circuits.
levels.expert:
**Pediatric exposures.** A toddler who may have swallowed a calcium channel blocker, β-blocker, sulfonylurea, clonidine or tricyclic needs emergency evaluation and observation, even if well, because effects (especially from sustained-release forms) can be delayed. Poison control guides observation duration.

**The ECG checklist in any cardiotoxic exposure:** rate, PR interval (AV block), QRS width and the terminal R in aVR (sodium channel blockade), QTc (potassium channel blockade), and rhythm (bidirectional VT points to digoxin). Repeat the ECG serially.

**Management principles:**
- Treat in parallel: calcium, glucagon or high-insulin therapy, vasopressors and pacing can be started together; call for ECMO early in refractory shock, because the drug will eventually clear if perfusion is maintained.
- In high-insulin therapy, monitor glucose and potassium very frequently and give dextrose to maintain normoglycemia.
- Wide-QRS sodium channel toxicity: give hypertonic sodium bicarbonate; avoid class IA and IC antiarrhythmics (they worsen sodium channel block); lidocaine is a second-line option.
- Torsades: magnesium, correct potassium, stop offending drugs; avoid further QT-prolonging agents.
- Seizures: benzodiazepines; avoid phenytoin.
- Digoxin: give Fab for life-threatening arrhythmias or significant hyperkalemia; treat hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia in chronic toxicity; review interacting drugs and kidney function.

**Medication safety lessons:** chronic digoxin toxicity in older adults after an illness reduces renal function; a new macrolide or amiodarone added to digoxin without adjustment; QT drugs stacked in hospitalized patients with low potassium. Pharmacist medication reconciliation and electronic interaction alerts prevent many of these.

**Neurosurgical relevance:** local anesthetic systemic toxicity can follow scalp blocks or large-volume infiltration; know where lipid emulsion is stored. Perioperative QT prolongation from antiemetics plus electrolyte shifts after subarachnoid hemorrhage is a real risk; monitor ECGs and electrolytes.

keyPoints: Mostly accidental pediatric ingestion, medication errors, interactions, kidney decline
Beta-blockers: bradycardia, hypoglycemia (children); glucagon, HIET
Calcium channel blockers: shock with hyperglycemia; calcium, HIET, ECMO
Digoxin: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; bidirectional VT, hyperkalemia (acute); digoxin Fab
Wide QRS (sodium channel) → bicarbonate; torsades → magnesium; LAST → lipid emulsion
